title: Barrowlight
intro:
Rain has followed you for three days across the Greywater moor. The villagers of Hollin's Rest would not say the barrow's name. They only pointed north and made the sign of the ash.

Somewhere beneath that mound lies the Barrowlight, the lantern the Ashen Order kept burning so their dead would sleep. It went dark at the turn of the season. Since then, the graves of Hollin's Rest have not stayed shut.

You crest the last hill as dusk bleeds out of the sky, and the lichgate rises before you.

epilogues.text:
The Great Vesper Bell rings once above the Cradle, clear and whole, and for the first time in three hundred years the sound is allowed to end.

Aurelius rises from Caelia's side as the amber thins to frost. She does not wake into pain. She opens her eyes long enough to find his face and say his name, and the old mason laughs and weeps at once, because he had forgotten her voice and now he will never forget it again. Then she goes into the warm gold light. He sits a long while beside the empty bier, and when at last he follows her across the threshold, he goes of his own will.

The Barrowlight stays behind in the Skull's cradle, where it was always meant to sit, and Sister Wren walks back up through the Nave at your side. In the Archive, Prelate Vaelen has unstrung the last wire of Lira's carillon and keeps the silver tine in her pocket, not to bind anything, only to remember the pitch. At the crossroads, Commander Silas has chalked every name of his garrison onto the wall, and beneath them, in a newer hand, the names of the dead who walked into the gold that week, so that someone will have witnessed them. None of the three is healed. All three are still here, and they chose to be.

Above, on Greywater moor, the graves of Hollin's Rest lie quiet in the rain, not chained, only finished. The villagers still make the sign of the ash when they speak of the barrow, but now they speak of it. When travelers ask who opened the third gate, the old women of the village say it was not one person. It was {player.name}, they say, and everyone {player.name} stopped to listen to on the way down.

"Last the face all faces yield," you say, and behind you a cracked old voice says it with you. Aurelius has waited three hundred years to finish the verse he chiseled out of the stone.

The amber over Caelia's bier dissolves like breath on a cold window. Her spirit lingers only a moment, a hand laid against his calcified cheek, and then she is gone into the warm gold light, and the bronze plates fall from the First Architect one by one until only a tired mason in a dusty apron kneels in the ash. He asks you for nothing. He stays to tend the Great Brazier he built, now that it finally does what it was meant to do.

Up through the Under-Barrow the change spreads slowly, the way a thaw does. The calcified dead of the upper tombs lie down and are still. The lucid dead of Nocturne go on living, remembering, and quarrelling in the Lantern Market, and when one of them is ready, they walk down the stair and do not come back, and their friends say the Rite of Rest after them. Not everyone you met below is there to see it. The Barrowlight, burning in the Skull's cradle, does not forget them either.

On Greywater moor the rain keeps falling and the graves of Hollin's Rest keep still. You walk out through the lichgate at dawn, {player.name}, with empty hands for the first time since you came to Greywater. Far below, the Barrowlight burns low and warm in the Great Brazier, the plain gold of a lamp that has nothing left to hold back.

The Rite of True Passage was meant to be spoken by the one who broke it. Aurelius lies in bronze pieces at the foot of the dais, so you speak it alone, and the Great Brazier takes the words anyway.

Gold light pours into the conduit-roots. The amber over Caelia's bier runs like warm honey and her breath goes out of her at last, and from the ruin of the First Architect a stooped shade in a mason's apron rises to meet her at the threshold. He looks back at you once. You never learn whether it was forgiveness, or only surprise that the thing he feared most was so quiet.

The Under-Barrow is freed by a hand that also broke it. The calcified dead rest. The lucid dead of Nocturne may walk into the gold when they are ready, and some of them will not forgive you for the wardens and the prelates and the commanders you cut down on the way, and they will be right not to. The Triad does not ask to be earned. It only asks to be completed.

You climb out through the lichgate into the rain, {player.name}, and leave the Barrowlight burning in the Skull's cradle far below. It burns gold, but there was ash on its glass when you set it down that would not wipe away, and you find you would rather the valley remember both than neither.

White fire climbs the roots of the mountain, and one by one the waking dead of the Under-Barrow lie down and close their eyes. Nocturne's lanterns gutter out. The Archive falls silent. The graves of Hollin's Rest stay shut.

But this time the sleep is kept by people who remember why. The Ashen Order you return to is not the one that sent its wardens into the dark with lye and iron. Its new keepers write their names on their helms instead of scouring them away, and they speak the Rite of Rest over every grave they close, as if the sleeper could hear. Perhaps they can. Some of the oldest wardens say they dream now, a little, at the edge of the light.

You know what the Great Vesper Bell knows: the stasis is a pressure, not a peace, and one day the bronze will crack again. So before you leave the deep, you pry the lead from the third socket of the frieze on the Stair of the Uncarved Skull and leave the old verse bare for whoever comes after: none is whole without the third.

It is a gentler cage, {player.name}, and you built it with your eyes open. On the long walk back across Greywater moor, you are never quite sure whether you saved the valley or only gave it more time. Perhaps, for now, those are the same thing.

You lock the Sun Seal into the grate and the Great Brazier roars white, and everything that was awake beneath Greywater stops.

The wraiths of the upper tombs fold back into the ash. The quarrelling, remembering, lantern-lit dead of Nocturne go still in the middle of their sentences. The Choir's wires hang slack over silent cylinders. No one below the lichgate will grieve again, because no one below the lichgate will remember enough to grieve. The Ashen Order calls it a miracle. Within the year they are calling you its Warden.

You take the title, {player.name}. Someone has to walk the circuit of the barrows and keep the fire fed, and you are very good at it, the way Ser Halric was very good at walking his circle in the ash. The villagers of Hollin's Rest bless your name. They never ask what it cost, and after a few winters you could not tell them, because the faces you met in the deep have begun to blur whenever the flame dips.

The Barrowlight burns ash-pale at your hip. Far below, the Great Vesper Bell holds its fracture in the dark, and waits.

Silver-blue light runs up through the roots of the mountain, and every spirit in the Under-Barrow feels its outline settle and hold. No one below the lichgate will fade into the dark again.

Nocturne's Lantern Market never closes now. The dead teach the living their old songs and their old recipes and the names of the hills before the barrow had a name, and the living write it all down. The Choir's wires come down from the cradles one by one, because nothing needs binding when nothing is slipping away. Those who learned below that a song may be allowed to end keep watch over those who never did.

The memory-salt still gathers. It drifts at the edges of the oldest minds like snow against a door, and some of them begin to repeat themselves, and then to repeat only one thing. When that happens, the Wayfarers sit with them and speak the Rite of Rest, and ask, and sometimes the answer is yes, and the Moon Seal does not stop them. The vigil is endless. It is not blind.

Some nights, standing beneath the silver lanterns, you wonder whether a song that cannot end is only noise. Then someone you met in the deep calls you by name, {player.name}, the {player.class} who came down the stair, and you choose again to keep listening.

You set the Moon Seal into the resonator, and the Great Brazier answers with a single silver chord that does not stop.

It does not stop in the Archive, where a Choir without its Prelate hears the endless note as vindication and winds every carillon tighter. It does not stop in the dark streets of Nocturne, where no beacon burns to show the dead which of them are still themselves. It does not stop in the minds of the ten thousand sleepers of Greywater, who wake all at once and find they cannot go back.

No one is lost. That was the promise, and the Moon keeps it. The memory-salt piles in drifts against the doors of the Lantern Market, and the spirits beneath it say the same last sentence over and over, word-perfect, forever. When you come back down the stair years later, a woman in a moth-eaten shawl greets you at the bottom with the same words she spoke the day you first passed her, and the day after that, and every day since.

You built a cradle out of grief, {player.name}, just as the First Architect did. The Barrowlight burns silver-blue at your hip, bright and cold, and it has not flickered once. It never will.

The Great Brazier falls quiet behind you, and whatever you chose there, you carry it up out of the deep alone.

The long stair gives way to the Weeping Stair, the stair to the barrow, the barrow to the lichgate and the rain. Greywater moor is as grey as you left it. The villagers of Hollin's Rest watch you come down the hill and make the sign of the ash, and do not ask.

The Barrowlight still burns at your hip, {player.name}. In time you may learn what its color means.

gameOverText: The cold of the barrow closes over you like deep water. Somewhere far above, rain falls on the lichgate, and the Barrowlight stays dark. Your story ends here, {player.name}.
